# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Terms.** By "biological father" I mean a man whose seed, by natural generation, contributed to the conception of the child. The standard reading is that Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no human father. Joseph was his legal and reputed father, not his begetter.

---

## 1. Matthew's genealogy breaks the begetting formula at Joseph

- [L1] Matthew 1:2-16 runs in one repeated pattern, "A begat B." Then verse 16 says: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, **of whom** was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] The verb throughout is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "he begat"), active voice, with the father as subject. In verse 16 the pattern stops. Joseph is not the subject of "begat." The verb becomes ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born"), passive. The relative pronoun is ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), **feminine singular**, so it can only refer to Mary. Joseph is described as ἄνδρα (andra, "husband"), not as begetter.
- [L4] Matthew keeps the begetting formula unbroken for every earlier generation and drops it only at Joseph. The grammar assigns the birth to the mother alone. That is a deliberate signal, not an accident. The footing is the active-to-passive shift and the feminine pronoun [L2], which governs verse 16 [L1].

## 2. The text names the source of the conception

- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child **of the Holy Ghost**." Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is **of the Holy Ghost**." Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] The phrase is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy"). The preposition ἐκ (ek, "out of") marks origin or source, the same preposition used of Mary in 1:16. Luke's ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow") describes divine power acting on her. It is not the language of marital union. The connective διό (dio, "therefore, for which reason") in Luke 1:35 makes the Holy Ghost's action the stated cause of the title "Son of God."
- [L1] Mary's own question rules out a human father: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34). The Greek is ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "I am not knowing a man"). The angel answers with the Holy Ghost, not with Joseph.
- [L3] The sign was foretold. Isaiah 7:14 reads הָעַלְמָה הָרָה (ha-ʻalmāh hārāh, "the young woman [is] with child, or shall conceive"). The Hebrew עַלְמָה (ʻalmāh) means a young woman of marriageable age. Matthew 1:22-23 quotes the verse as fulfilled, and the Greek παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin") fixes its sense. Luke 1:27 independently calls Mary a παρθένον (parthenon, "virgin") before the conception.

## 3. Joseph is excluded as begetter, and is called father only by reputation

- [L1] Matthew 1:19-20: Joseph "was minded to put her away privily" on finding her with child. An angel then explains that the conception is "of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:25: "[Joseph] knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L2] ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing," imperfect, a continued state) ... ἕως (heōs, "until") shows that no marital relations preceded the birth.
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "Jesus ... being (**as was supposed**) the son of Joseph." The Greek is ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was thought, reckoned"), which marks a popular opinion, not a fact. John 6:42 shows the crowd holding that opinion: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?"
- [L3] Luke 2:48-49 has Mary say "thy father and I have sought thee," and the child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about **my Father's** business?" Mary uses the reputed, legal sense. The child's reply corrects the ground of the sonship. Luke 2:33 ("Joseph and his mother marvelled") also distinguishes Joseph from the true father.

## 4. The wider witness: "of a woman," "her seed," "a body prepared"

- [L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, **made of a woman**." [L2] γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman") names the woman alone as the human source.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15 speaks of "**her** seed." The Hebrew is זַרְעָהּ (zarʻāh, "her seed"). Seed is normally reckoned through the man, and here it is reckoned through the woman. Hebrews 10:5 says "a body hast thou prepared me." The Greek is σῶμα κατηρτίσω (sōma katērtisō, "a body you fitted together"), which attributes the preparation of the body to God.
- [L4] Scripture assigns the human origin to the woman and the preparation of the body to God, not to a human father. The footing is Galatians 4:4 [L1/L2] and Genesis 3:15 with Hebrews 10:5 [L3]. The inference is that these verses are consistent with the explicit statements in sections 1-3.

## 5. Why the biological line through Joseph would contradict Scripture

- [L1] Matthew 1:11-12 places Jechonias in the line that ends with Joseph. Jeremiah 22:30 says of Jechonias (Coniah): "no man of **his seed** shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."
- [L2] The Hebrew is מִזַּרְעוֹ (mizzarʻô, "from his seed"). It is a statement about descent.
- [L4] If Joseph were the biological father, Jesus would be of Jechonias's seed and would fall under that judgment. Yet Luke 1:32-33 says he receives "the throne of his father David" and reigns "for ever." The two verses are reconciled if Joseph's line gives the legal right (Matthew 1:16) and Mary's body gives the actual descent. The footing is Jeremiah 22:30 [L1/L2] and Luke 1:32-33 with Matthew 1:11-16 [L1/L3].
- [L3] "Father" in Luke 1:32 and "son of David" in Matthew 1:1 are ancestral uses. Scripture commonly calls a forefather "father" (compare Luke 1:73, "our father Abraham"). This answers the objection from Romans 1:3 ("of the seed of David according to the flesh"). That verse says the descent is through the flesh, but it does not say through Joseph's seed.

## 6. The objection from "Father" and "begotten"

- [L1] John 1:14 says "the only begotten of the Father." Luke 1:35 says "the power of the Highest" and "Son of God."
- [L2] μονογενής (monogenēs, "only-born, one of a kind") describes a unique relation. The Holy Ghost's action in Luke 1:35 is the conception of the human nature. It is not a physical union and does not make God a biological father in the sense defined above.
- [L4] The title "Son of God" in Luke 1:35 rests on the action of the Highest [L1] and on the causal διό [L2]. This is a divine and unique origin. It is not a human paternity of seed, so the denial of a biological father stands.

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the begetting formula at Joseph: the active ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") gives way to the passive ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born") with the feminine ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), so the birth is assigned to Mary alone. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:2-16; [L2] the active-to-passive shift and the feminine relative pronoun.
2. The conception is stated to be ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy"), by the overshadowing power of the Highest, in one who "knew not a man," and was foretold. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20 and Luke 1:34-35; [L2] ek, ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow"), and διό (dio, "therefore"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 with Matthew 1:22-23 and Luke 1:27.
3. Joseph is excluded as begetter and is called father only by reputation. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:19, 25 and Luke 3:23; [L2] ἐγίνωσκεν ... ἕως (eginōsken ... heōs, "was knowing ... until") and ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed"); [L3] John 6:42 and Luke 2:48-49.
4. The wider witness assigns the human origin to the woman alone and the preparation of the body to God. Footing: [L1] Galatians 4:4; [L2] γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman") and זַרְעָהּ (zarʻāh, "her seed"); [L3] Genesis 3:15 and Hebrews 10:5.
5. A biological descent through Joseph would bring Jesus under Jeremiah 22:30, which conflicts with Luke 1:32-33. The legal right through Joseph and the actual descent through Mary resolve it. Footing: [L1] Jeremiah 22:30, Matthew 1:11-16 and Luke 1:32-33; [L2] מִזַּרְעוֹ (mizzarʻô, "from his seed"); [L3] ancestral "father" at Luke 1:73 and Matthew 1:1.
6. Answer to the topic question: No. Christ had no biological father. He was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, Joseph was his legal and reputed father only, and "Son of God" names a unique divine origin, not a human begetting. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16, 18, 20, Luke 1:34-35 and Luke 3:23; [L2] ἐξ ἧς (ex hēs, "out of whom"), ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy") and ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed"); [L3] Isaiah 7:14 and Galatians 4:4.

# CHALLENGER — the record's reading pressed against the chain

The defender's case turns one birth-narration verb into a denial, one origin phrase into a paternity, and one prophet's sign into a proof of no father. The seed rows will not bear it. I press the chain link by link and put the keystone last.

---

## PRESS ON LINK 1 — Matthew 1:16

**Target stated:** "The grammar assigns the birth to the mother alone. That is a deliberate signal... to no human father."

**Counter-witness, quoted:**

[L1] Romans 1:3 — "Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the **seed of David according to the flesh**."
[L1] Acts 2:30 — "of the **fruit of his loins**, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 — "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed **out of thy bowels**."
[L1] Psalm 132:11 — "Of the **fruit of thy body** will I set upon thy throne."
[L1] Hebrews 7:14 — "it is **evident** that our Lord **sprang out of Juda**."

One sentence each: Romans 1:3 states the descent is seed of David by the flesh; Acts 2:30 states it as fruit of his loins by the flesh; 2 Samuel 7:12 defines that seed as proceeding out of a man's bowels; Psalm 132:11 as fruit of the body; Hebrews 7:14 calls the springing out of Judah **evident**.

**The passive is narration, not denial.** [L2] egennēthē (G1080, "was born") is the ordinary word for being borne by a mother — the same event Matthew 1:25 narrates in the words "she had brought forth her firstborn son." A passive that states where the birth came from says nothing about where the begetting came from; it does not say "no man." Against 39 active egennēsen tokens the defence reads the one passive as a verdict on the father. [L1] Matthew 1:16 itself calls Joseph "the husband of Mary," and [L1] Matthew 1:20 calls him "Joseph, thou son of David," and [L1] Matthew 1:21, 25 give **him** the naming act — "thou shalt call his name JESUS," "he called his name JESUS."

**The canon's stated means of begetting.** [L1] Genesis 4:1 — "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." [L1] Genesis 3:15 speaks of "her seed" of that same Eve — whose seed came by that knowing. The four woman-seed rows in the whole canon are Genesis 3:15, 16:10 (Hagar), 24:60 (Rebekah), Isaiah 54:3 (Zion); none is Davidic, and in every one of them a man is named as the begetter.

**Footing:** [L1] Romans 1:3; Acts 2:30; 2 Samuel 7:12; Psalm 132:11; Hebrews 7:14; Matthew 1:16, 20, 21, 25; Genesis 3:15; 4:1. [L2] egennēthē passive = borne, not begat. **LINK 1 is contradicted at [L1] by five seed rows it never engages.**

---

## PRESS ON LINK 2 — "of the Holy Ghost"

**Target stated:** ek pneumatos hagiou "marks origin or source... Luke's episkiasis describes divine power acting on her. It is not the language of marital union."

**Counter-witness on ek:** [L2] ek (G1537, "out of") with God or the Spirit is the covenant-origin idiom everywhere it appears: [L1] John 1:13 "born of God"; 1 John 3:9 "born of God"; 1 John 4:7 "is of God"; 1 John 5:1 "born of God." Not one of those rows means God biologically fathered the believer. When Paul means flesh, he says so by adding kata sarka: [L1] Romans 1:3 "ek spermatos Dauid **kata sarka**." [L2] Matthew 1:20 has no kata sarka. The defender's own canon answers the gloss.

**Counter-witness on the two verbs:**
[L1] Acts 1:8 — "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is **come upon** (eperchomai, G1904) you." Spoken to the apostles, who were already born. [L1] Luke 24:49 "the promise of my Father upon you." Come upon = anointing and presence at all 10 rows.
[L1] Acts 5:15 — "they brought forth the sick... that at the least the **shadow** of Peter... might overshadow (episkiazō, G1982) some of them." The other rows are the transfiguration cloud, [L1] Matthew 17:5; Mark 9:7; Luke 9:34. At its 5 rows the verb is presence, cloud, shadow — never begetting.

**Counter-witness on Luke 1:34:** [L2] andra ou ginōskō (G1097, "I am not knowing a man") is **present active indicative** — her state when the angel spoke. A permanent vow would take ou me with an aorist subjunctive. [L1] Luke 2:48 is the same woman's own mouth: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

**Counter-witness on Isaiah 7:14:** [L2] the Hebrew word is ha-almah (H5959, "the young woman"), 7 rows; bethulah (H1330, "the virgin") is the word for a virgin and is used 50 times across 19 books, 9 of them in the Torah. The prophecy's own frame bounds the sign in Isaiah's day: [L1] Isaiah 7:16 "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken"; 8:8 "...O Immanuel." The prophecy does not by itself state no-father; the defender imports that from outside it.

**The title in that verse is not paternity.** [L1] Luke 1:32-33 gives "the throne of his father David" **before** the question in 1:34, and [L1] 1:35 says "shall be **called** the Son of God." [L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6 — "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him to **be my son**, and I will be his father" — of a man whose father was David. [L1] Acts 13:33 applies "this day have I begotten thee" (Psalm 2:7) to the **resurrection**; [L1] Romans 1:4 "declared to be the Son of God... by the resurrection."

**Footing:** [L1] John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 4:7; 5:1; Romans 1:3; Acts 1:8; 5:15; 13:33; Luke 24:49; Matthew 17:5; Luke 9:34; Luke 1:32-35; 2:48; 1 Chronicles 28:6; Isaiah 7:16; 8:8. [L2] ek + God = covenant origin; kata sarka marks flesh; eperchomai, episkiazō measured at every row; almah (H5959) vs bethulah (H1330). **LINK 2 is contradicted by the word-level rows it claims.**

---

## PRESS ON LINK 3 — Joseph "excluded as begetter"

**Target stated:** Matthew 1:25 shows "no marital relations preceded the birth"; Luke 3:23 marks "a popular opinion, not a fact."

**Counter-witness — the father named in four registers:**
[L1] Mary — "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48).
[L1] The narrator — "the **parents** brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27); "his parents went to Jerusalem" (2:41); "Joseph and his mother marvelled" (2:33).
[L1] The town — "Is not this the son of Joseph?" (Luke 4:22); "Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" (John 6:42).
[L1] The angel — "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20); "Joseph was of the house of David" (Luke 1:27); "of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4).

**Counter-witness — the law's own words for the pair:** [L1] Matthew 1:19 "Joseph **her husband**"; 1:20 "Mary **thy wife**"; [L1] Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's **wife**." To part he must "put her away" (1:19). [L1] Matthew 1:24 "took unto him his wife"; 1:25 "knew her not **till** she had brought forth her firstborn son" — "till" bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy, and "firstborn son" is ordinary birth language.

**The timing rows, stated as the text writes them and read in that chain:** [L1] Matthew 1:18 "before they came together, she was found with child" dates the **finding**, not the begetting; [L1] Matthew 1:25 as quoted; [L1] Luke 1:34 as quoted above, present tense. On the footing of "Joseph her husband" (Matthew 1:19), "Mary thy wife" (1:20), "his neighbour's wife" (Deuteronomy 22:24), and "till" (1:25), the inference carried at [L4] is that **Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal** — that is the reading I press, and it is the reading those rows support. None of the conception rows, Matthew 1:18-25 or Luke 1:26-38, says she conceived without a man.

**Counter-witness on enomizeto:** [L2] enomizeto (G3543, "was wont, was reckoned") is the same form as [L1] Acts 16:13 "where prayer **was wont** to be made." The word carries no verdict of its own; and here it stands beside [L1] Luke 2:48 and [L1] John 6:42, both of which name Joseph as father in ordinary speech, "whose father and mother we know."

**Footing:** [L1] Luke 1:27; 2:4, 27, 33, 41, 48; 4:22; John 6:42; Matthew 1:18, 19, 20, 24, 25; Deuteronomy 22:24; Acts 16:13; Genesis 4:1. [L2] enomizeto = "wont"; ou ginōskō present. **LINK 3 is contradicted by the naming rows and by the text's own marriage vocabulary.**

---

## PRESS ON LINK 4 — "made of a woman," "her seed"

**Target stated:** "Scripture assigns the human origin to the woman... not to a human father."

**Counter-witness on Galatians 4:4:** [L1] Job 14:1 — "man that is **born of a woman**"; Job 15:14; Job 25:4 — "how can he be clean that is **born of a woman**?"; [L1] Matthew 11:11 — "Among them that are **born of women** there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist" — of John, **whose father is named** ("thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son... and thou shalt call his name John," Luke 1:13). The phrase is the mortality idiom, not a no-father idiom.

**Counter-witness on Genesis 3:15:** "her seed" is said of Eve, and the same book states how her seed came: [L1] Genesis 4:1 "Adam knew **his wife**; and she conceived." [L2] zar'ah (H2233, "seed") with a feminine suffix is not a begetting formula. The four woman-seed rows are Genesis 3:15, 16:10, 24:60, Isaiah 54:3 — Hagar, Rebekah, Zion — each with a named man.

**Counter-witness on Hebrews 10:5:** [L1] "a body hast thou prepared me" states who assembles the body; it does not state that no man begets. God prepares every body — [L1] Psalm 139:13-16 "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb... in thy book all my members were written" — of men with fathers. And [L1] Hebrews 7:10 says Levi was "in the loins of his father"; [L1] Hebrews 7:14 says our Lord "sprang out of Juda," the tribe counted [L1] Numbers 1:2, 18 "by the house of their fathers."

**Footing:** [L1] Job 14:1; 15:14; 25:4; Matthew 11:11; Luke 1:13; Genesis 3:15; 4:1; 16:10; 24:60; Isaiah 54:3; Psalm 139:13-16; Hebrews 7:10, 14; Numbers 1:2, 18. [L2] zar'ah with feminine suffix; "born of a woman" = mortality. **LINK 4's [L4] floats: it turns a mortality idiom and one woman-seed verse into an exclusion the words do not make.**

---

## PRESS ON LINK 5 — Jeremiah 22:30

**Target stated:** "If Joseph were the biological father, Jesus would be of Jechonias's seed and would fall under that judgment... reconciled if Joseph's line gives the legal right and Mary's body gives the actual descent."

**Counter-witness, four rows:**

[L1] Jeremiah 22:30 is bounded in its own words: "a man that shall not prosper **in his days**: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more **in Judah**."
[L1] Jeremiah 18:7-8 — "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will **repent** of the evil that I thought to do unto them." The prophet's own rule on pronounced sentences.
[L1] Haggai 2:23 — the signet plucked at Jeremiah 22:24 is set again: "I will take thee, O Zerubbabel... my servant... and will make thee as a signet." [L1] Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1 name him **governor**, never king. The sentence is answered in the same prophet's book.
[L1] 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 — Jeconiah's sons are numbered, seven of them.

And the New Testament never cites this curse against the one who receives "the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32). Iechonias appears twice in the whole New Testament (Matthew 1:11, 12) and no apostle pleads Jeremiah 22:30 against the throne promised at Luke 1:32-33.

**The resolution itself floats.** "Mary's body gives the actual descent" is asserted with no text: no verse states Mary's descent from David. What is stated is [L1] Luke 1:36, where her kinswoman Elisabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron" (1:5). A resolution that must import an unstated lineage to escape a curse that is never applied is an [L4] resting on one layer only.

**Footing:** [L1] Jeremiah 22:24, 30; 18:7-8; Haggai 1:1; 2:23; Ezra 3:2; 1 Chronicles 3:17-18; Matthew 1:11-12; Luke 1:5, 32-36. **LINK 5 is contradicted as applied and floats as resolved.**

---

## PRESS ON LINK 6 — the keystone: "Christ had no biological father"

The keystone is stated as fact. Set against it:

[L1] Romans 1:3 — "made of the **seed of David according to the flesh**."
[L1] Acts 2:30 — "of the **fruit of his loins, according to the flesh**."
[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 — "which shall proceed **out of thy bowels**."
[L1] Psalm 132:11 — "Of the **fruit of thy body** will I set upon thy throne."
[L1] Hebrews 7:14 — "it is **evident** that our Lord sprang out of Juda."
[L1] Luke 1:32 — "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of **his father David**."
[L1] John 6:42 — "the son of Joseph, **whose father and mother we know**."
[L1] Luke 2:48 — "thy **father** and I have sought thee sorrowing."
[L1] Genesis 4:1 — "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."

Seven of these say seed out of a man's body by the flesh, or name the father outright. A conclusion that requires seed out of loins to be true cannot coexist with "no biological father." The title "Son of God" does not carry the keystone either: [L1] 2 Samuel 7:14 "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" is spoken of Solomon, and [L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6 names Solomon "thy son" and "my son" in one breath, with David his father. [L1] Acts 13:33 places the begetting at the resurrection.

**Footing:** [L1] as quoted; [L2] kata sarka marks flesh at Romans 1:3; osphys (G3751, "the loins") at Acts 2:30 is the same word as Hebrews 7:5, 10. **D6 is broken at [L1] and [L2].**

---

## UNSUPPORTED-[L4] PREMISES — defender's words, verbatim

1. **D1:** "The grammar assigns the birth to the mother alone. That is a deliberate signal, not an accident." — The step from the passive verb to "mother alone" as an exclusion of a father exhibits no second layer; the counter rows are Romans 1:3; Acts 2:30; 2 Samuel 7:12; Genesis 4:1. Unsupported.
2. **D4:** "Scripture assigns the human origin to the woman and the preparation of the body to God, not to a human father." — Exhibits only Galatians 4:4, Genesis 3:15, Hebrews 10:5; Job 14:1; Matthew 11:11; Genesis 4:1; Psalm 139:13 stand against it. Unsupported.
3. **D5:** "The two verses are reconciled if Joseph's line gives the legal right (Matthew 1:16) and Mary's body gives the actual descent." — No verse states Mary's descent; Luke 1:5, 36 name her kinswoman "of the daughters of Aaron." One layer, and that layer points elsewhere. Unsupported.
4. **D5:** "That verse says the descent is through the flesh, but it does not say through Joseph's seed." — Romans 1:3 says "the seed of David according to the flesh"; Acts 2:30 says "the fruit of his loins"; the silence being claimed is manufactured by reading one register out. Unsupported.
5. **D6:** "This is a divine and unique origin. It is not a human paternity of seed." — Built on Luke 1:35 alone, with 1 Chronicles 28:6; 2 Samuel 7:14; Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4 unanswered. Unsupported.
6. **D2:** the claim that ek pneumatos hagiou marks biological origin — John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 4:7; 5:1 use the same idiom of believers, and Romans 1:3 adds kata sarka when flesh is meant. Unsupported.

---

## Closing

The chain's strength is in its grammar; the record's answer is in its seed. [L1] Romans 1:3 and Acts 2:30 say **according to the flesh**; [L1] 2 Samuel 7:12 and Psalm 132:11 say **out of thy bowels, fruit of thy body**; [L1] Hebrews 7:14 says the springing out of Judah is **evident**; [L1] Mary says "thy father," the town says "whose father and mother we know," the angel says "Joseph, thou son of David" and gives **him** the naming. The two rows the defender leans on — [L1] Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 — are held as written and they date a **finding** and bound an abstinence to a pregnancy; [L1] Luke 1:34 is present tense. Read inside the marriage the text states ("Joseph her husband," Matthew 1:19; "Mary thy wife," 1:20; "his neighbour's wife," Deuteronomy 22:24), those rows carry the inference at [L4] that Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal. On the footing exhibited above, **D6 is broken, and D1, D2, D4, D5 stand contradicted at [L1] and [L2].** The topic's answer, on these verses: **yes — a man was named, and the seed is out of his loins.**

# Defender, Round 2: the chain re-seated

The challenger answers with a pile of seed rows. Each one says "seed," "loins," or "flesh," and none names an immediate begetter. Each is answered by re-seating it in its chain. The chain's keystone is Matthew 1:18-25 with Luke 1:26-38, and the challenger's counter-chain has to break there.

---

## 1. Matthew 1:16-25 as one block (answers Links 1 and 3)

**The passive verb.** The challenger says ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was begotten/born") "states where the birth came from" and "says nothing about where the begetting came from."
